text:
A 33-year-old office worker in Seoul’s Yongsan District surnamed Lee signed up for an app that lets her pay rent by credit card, after hearing about the service in a news report. Rent takes up a large share of her monthly budget, she said, and having enough cash on hand by the due date can be stressful.
“I like that paying by card buys me time until the bill comes due,” Lee said. “I’m still weighing whether that’s worth the fee.”
Rent payment apps are gaining ground as housing costs rise, particularly in Seoul, and more landlords switch from "jeonse," or large lump-sum leases, to monthly rentals.
The services allow renters who are short on cash to cover their rent if they have enough available credit, but some providers charge fees exceeding 7 percent of the payment amount. Reports of landlords failing to receive rent on time even after tenants have paid by card have also raised consumer protection concerns.
The average monthly rent for a Seoul apartment reached 1.68 million won ($1,260) in October, up 190,000 won from the end of last year, according to the Korea Real Estate Board. Over the same period, average monthly rent in low-rise multifamily homes rose by 42,000 won to 684,000 won.
Homes Pay and Zipup Pay have each surpassed 10,000 downloads on Google Play.
Kim Ki-tae, CEO of DEVD, which operates Zipup Pay, told a local media outlet that the idea grew out of a simple question: If people could pay for meals and transportation by credit card, why did they still have to pay rent, often their biggest monthly expense, by bank transfer?
New providers are also entering the market. Lanseon Pay, which launched its app last month, lets tenants pay rent in installments over a period of up to 24 months. Users enter the recipient’s bank account number and the amount they want to send, then pay by credit card. The company says the money typically reaches the recipient’s account in about five minutes.
Credit card issuers introduced their own rent payment services in 2019 after the Financial Services Commission designated card-based rent payments as an innovative financial service under its regulatory sandbox.
Those services require landlords to register with the issuer in much the same way merchants do. The newer apps charge the tenant’s card for the rent plus a service fee, then transfer the rent to the landlord’s bank account. Providers say tenants can use the apps without seeking their landlord’s consent or asking them to register.
Rent payment services typically charge between 2 and 4 percent, with some providers charging 7 percent or more. For a tenant paying Seoul’s average apartment rent, that translates to about 67,000 won in fees at 4 percent, or nearly 118,000 won at 7 percent.
Paying by card also leaves tenants dependent on the provider to complete the transfer. In one online community post, a tenant reported paying two months’ rent by credit card through a rent payment service and receiving a payment demand from the landlord after the transfer was delayed.
The services also raise questions about how they handle landlords’ personal information. One issue is whether providers meet legal requirements for collecting and using landlords’ bank account details when tenants enter them into an app.
